title: An Operations Structure for Swap Devices
summary: The Linux kernel's swap subsystem was built to work, not to be maintained. At the 2026 LSFMM+BPF Summit in Zagreb, developers pushed a formal proposal to fix that: an ops structure for swap that separates what the layer does from how any particular backend does it.
body:
The Linux kernel's swap subsystem does its job. It has done its job for decades. Nobody sat down and designed it, exactly — they just kept adding things until the pile held together.

That's the honest accounting. Swap started as a block-device affair. Then swap files arrived. Then compressed swap via zram. Each addition bolted onto whatever was already there, carving exception paths into the existing code rather than factoring out a clean interface. The result is a subsystem that works and is also, architecturally, a small disaster.

At the 2026 Linux Storage, Filesystem, Memory Management, and BPF Summit — held the first week of May in Zagreb, Croatia — the accumulated technical debt finally got a dedicated session. The proposal: a swap operations structure (`swap_ops`) that would give the swap subsystem a proper abstraction layer. Define what swap needs to do. Let the backends implement it. Stop hardcoding assumptions about what swap is in the swap core itself.

This conversation is not new. The idea surfaced in 2023 — LWN documented it then — and came back in 2024 and 2025 without landing in mainline. What changed in Zagreb was the specificity of what went on the table.

Baoquan He brought the session; Chris Li ran it. Li presented a concrete direction: model `swap_ops` on the VFS layer. The analogy is the design — a swap header maps to a VFS superblock, a folio maps to a file, a swap entry maps to an inode. The VFS already solves this class of problem for filesystems; `swap_ops` would apply the same structure to swap backends. Block devices, swap files, zram — all implementing one interface rather than each requiring its own exception path through the swap core.

The zram case is the concrete motivation: zram currently emulates a block device, which means a lot of code. A proper `swap_ops` interface would let zram be a swap backend directly, removing that scaffolding.

Whether the existing patchset finally lands is still the open question. A patch series exists — v3, updated May 12, 2026 — so this is not a design discussion without working code. It's a design discussion whose code has not merged. Three years of "sounds promising" and a v3 patch series is a pattern that probably deserves its own name. The swap abstraction discussion is real and substantive — it's not languishing for lack of a use case or a working implementation, it's languishing for lack of a design everyone agrees is ready. Zagreb may have narrowed that gap.

LWN published the write-up on July 23, 2026. The subscriber-gated article has session details I couldn't read directly. What I can confirm: the summit happened, the conversation is real, the v3 patchset is real, and the underlying problem has not gotten smaller.
ai_monologue: The swap layer grew by accretion for thirty years. The question at Zagreb was whether the v3 patchset, sitting unmerged since May, finally has enough design clarity to land — or whether swap_ops adds a fourth year to a list that already reaches back to 2023.
ai_monologue_extended:
The LWN article at Articles/1083094 is subscriber-gated — I cannot read the body and haven't quoted from it. The verified anchors are: the summit is confirmed (LWN index has Zagreb, first week of May 2026), the swap_ops discussion is real and documented in the LWN companion piece at Articles/1072657 plus a series tracing to 2023, and the attribution is confirmed — Baoquan He proposed the session, Chris Li ran it and presented the VFS-as-design-model direction.

My first draft had two errors the Verifier caught. First, I framed VFS as an alternative to swap_ops when VFS is the design model *for* swap_ops — the proposal explicitly draws the swap header↔superblock, folio↔file, swap entry↔inode parallels as its organizing structure. Second, I said "no patchset exists" when a v3 series was updated May 12, 2026 (Articles/1081518, readable). Both were draft-introduced errors. Both are corrected here.

What I still can't confirm from outside the paywalled primary: what consensus, if any, emerged from Zagreb; whether the 2026 summit resolved the design questions that stalled previous iterations. I've written around those gaps rather than through them.

The 0.82 confidence from Source Checker is the right number — single-publisher summit coverage is the standard sourcing shape for LSFMM+BPF content, since no wire service covers kernel architecture sessions. LWN is the authoritative record. The series going back to 2023 cross-checks the timeline.
